subject: zoology_2
question_text: Give an account of synaptic transmission.

mark_split.label: What a synapse is and its two types

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.33, SAQ 21. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Text revision (examiner audit, 2026-09-05): the insider note's claim that an out-of-order answer loses marks was replaced with the reason for writing the steps in order.

steps.label: What a synapse is
steps.why: Two neurons never touch, so the signal has to cross a junction, and how it crosses depends on how wide that junction is.
common_mistakes: Calling a synapse a kind of neuron. It is the junction between two.
Naming only the chemical type. Two types are expected.
steps.memory_tip: Electrical synapse: almost touching. Chemical synapse: a gap with a messenger.
steps.margin_note: Definition, then both types on separate lines.
lines: A synapse is the junction between two
successive neurons. It transmits nerve
impulses from one neuron to the next.
There are two types of synapses.
In an electrical synapse the membranes of
the two neurons lie very close and are
electrically conductive links.

steps.label: The chemical synapse
steps.why: A gap the signal cannot jump forces the neuron to send a chemical across instead of a current.
common_mistakes: Writing that the impulse jumps the cleft. A chemical carries it across.
steps.memory_tip: Cleft, vesicles, neurotransmitter — the three names of the chemical synapse.
steps.margin_note: Name the cleft and the vesicles. Both are marked.
lines: In a chemical synapse the two membranes
are separated by a fluid filled space
called the synaptic cleft.
Chemical messengers called
neurotransmitters carry the impulse across.
They are released from the synaptic
vesicles of the axon terminals.

steps.label: Calcium and exocytosis
steps.why: Calcium entering the terminal is the switch that turns an electrical signal into a chemical one.
common_mistakes: Naming sodium instead of calcium. Calcium channels open at the terminal.
Leaving out exocytosis. It is the marked word for the release.
steps.memory_tip: Impulse arrives, calcium in, vesicles fuse, transmitter out.
steps.margin_note: Four steps in order. Keep them as separate lines.
lines: When an impulse reaches the axon terminal,
the membrane gets depolarised and voltage
gated calcium channels open.
Calcium ions move the synaptic vesicles to
the membrane.
The vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane
and release their neurotransmitters into
the cleft by exocytosis.

steps.label: Receptors and new potential
steps.why: The transmitter opens gates on the next neuron, so a chemical signal becomes an electrical one again and the impulse continues.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the release. The answer must reach the next neuron.
Leaving out acetylcholine as the usual transmitter.
steps.memory_tip: Bind, gates open, ions in, new potential.
steps.margin_note: End at the new potential. That is where the impulse continues.
lines: The released neurotransmitters, mostly
acetylcholine, bind to their own receptors
on the post-synaptic membrane.
That membrane has ligand gated channels.

lines.text: Ions enter and make a new potential

insider_note: Follow the impulse in order: arrive, calcium in, vesicles fuse, transmitter out, receptor binds, new potential. Written in that order, each line follows from the one before it.
